‘The penchant for treating founders as god-kings whose companies are mere extensions of their visionary genius is a large part of the story underlying Musk's (and others') precipitous rise, but it's not only a credulous media and easily swayed investors who are to blame. In one especially telling episode, Musk invests in the electric-car startup Tesla, accuses its co-founder and CEO Martin Eberhard of fraud, then settles a libel lawsuit from Eberhard with the explicit stipulation that Musk be allowed to falsely call himself one of the company's original founders. (He made his first investment six months after Tesla was incorporated.) He claimed that zero-emission vehicles were part of his mission to stave off ecological collapse while exploiting tax credits for a battery-swap technology he knew was unworkable at scale. He also pushed self-driving technology that has been implicated in dozens of fatal crashes. In a deposition in one lawsuit over a 2018 crash, Ashok Elluswamy, the director of Tesla's Autopilot software, said that the company knowingly released a promotional video that presented self-driving's potential as if it had already been realized, effectively selling science fiction as science fact.
"Could it be," Gibney's narration asks, "that the world's richest man was also its most flamboyant fraud?"’
